articles.title: ‘Exceedingly heavy-handed’: ACT police criticised by magistrate for Tasering disabled Aboriginal woman
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Body-worn camera footage shows woman pulled off bench and a Taser activated despite ‘putting up no resistance’, magistrate says

  • Get our
articles.byline: Nino Bucci Justice and courts reporter

blocks.text: A magistrate has criticised “exceedingly heavy-handed” ACT police officers who Tasered an Aboriginal woman with an intellectual disability during a routine arrest.
The woman, named Emma, pleaded with officers not to use the stun gun on her and told them she was unarmed during the arrest at a Canberra bus stop in January.
Police were called because of reports Emma had a knife, but she was only found to have two pairs of scissors, one of which was broken, in a nearby backpack.
Guardian Australia is not using Emma’s full name at the request of her lawyer to protect her privacy.
The court was shown police body-worn footage of the arrest, in which she is seen raising her hands immediately after officers arrived and pointed a Taser towards her.
As she pushed back against an officer who was trying to handcuff her she was pulled to the ground.
While two officers held her down another placed a Taser against her back and activated it, in what is known as “drive stun” mode. Seven officers were present at the time.

The ACT magistrates court heard in September that officers also threatened to use OC spray against Emma after she appeared to self-harm by deliberately striking her head against a police van during the arrest.
A transcript of the hearing was released by the court to Guardian Australia in October.

Special magistrate Sean Richter, a former South Australian police officer, said he found the conduct of officers “incredibly” and “exceedingly” heavy-handed, and agreed that they were aware of who Emma was and her vulnerabilities before they arrested her.
“I sometimes wonder when we lost the ability to speak to people,” Richter said.
“She’s a woman that was putting up no resistance.
“She’s sitting on the bench with her arms in the air.”
Richter said Emma was involved in a motor vehicle accident when she was 12 and received a traumatic brain injury.
He said the ACT civil and administrative tribunal described her as having a mental impairment and a neurocognitive disorder, and said she had been placed on a psychiatric treatment order.

Emma was charged with multiple offences by police in relation to the incident, but all of them except possessing a knife without reasonable excuse were withdrawn by the prosecution. She pleaded guilty to that offence, which related to the scissors in her bag, and was convicted. Emma also faced Richter on other matters unrelated to the arrest.

“I was shown the video of her arrest on the charge of possess knife without reasonable excuse. I will say this; I consider that the actions of the police in that matter were unwarranted and heavy-handed,” Richter said.
“Here was a woman sitting on a park bench putting her arms in the air. She’s clearly known to the police because one of them names her.

“It’s blatantly apparent to anyone that deals with this woman that she has a significant cognitive disorder and should be treated as such. I find it amazing that in this day and age the police reacted in the way that they did.”
In a statement, ACT policing said it “notes the comments of Special Magistrate Richter in relation to the arrest of a woman in January 2026.
“As an associated civil claim is under way in relation to this matter, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment.”
after newsletter promotion
In that civil claim filed in July, Emma’s lawyer, Michael Lalor, accused one of the officers involved in the arrest of misfeasance in public office.

The officer is accused of making a series of misleading statements or omissions in police evidence that resulted in more serious charges being laid, and Emma spending 28 days in custody before bail was granted after her lawyers viewed the body-worn camera footage of the arrest.

The statement of claim alleges the misleading statements include that Emma ignored police commands, that she had “abruptly” bent down towards her bag, that she attempted to strike an officer multiple times in the face, and that she was Tasered because she engaged in a “high level of violence”.
Lalor also writes in the civil claim that it would be alleged police provided misleading statements regarding the witness who called officers saying they had seen a woman with a knife.

Police said that the civilian witness had “immediately feared for his safety and departed swiftly” after seeing Emma, but the statement of claim said police failed to make clear the man and his partner “were inside a moving vehicle with the doors locked at the relevant time”.
That witness also told police, according to the statement of claim, that “I wasn’t particularly scared, I was in a car with the doors locked, so I knew she couldn’t really stab me.”
Lalor is also alleging breaches of the Human Rights Act and exemplary damages for assault and battery.
Police have not yet been required to file a defence to the claim.
ACT police have come under repeated recent scrutiny for their use of force, particularly against Aboriginal people.

In August, the commonwealth and ACT ombudsman criticised police for failing to clearly define “racial profiling” after officers in Canberra pulled guns on an Indigenous teenager they mistook for a suspect in an aggravated burglary.

In June last year, the ACT ombudsman found that in about a third of cases it reviewed, unprofessional behaviour by officers such as impatience, aggression, foul and abusive language appeared to unnecessarily escalate situations.
This led to “use of force in circumstances where a more sensitive and trauma-informed approach to negotiation and de-escalation might have avoided the need to use force or as much force”.

As part of that investigation, the ombudsman recommended that police identify and implement measures to better equip its officers with a greater understanding of “mental illness and how it affects a person’s behaviour and ability to comply with directions”, but police did not accept the recommendation.

articles.title: ‘Settle down’, ‘do your own swabs’: how alleged rape victims are treated in Queensland revealed in major report
articles.summary:
Prosecutors dropped cases because survivors ‘didn’t act how a rape victim should’, Australian Institute of Criminology review of 19,000 sexual assault cases finds

  • Get our

blocks.text: Queensland police put sexual assault investigations “on the backburner” because detectives were overworked and under pressure to prioritise cases linked to political issues such as youth crime, a major new study has found.

The report, published this month by the Australian Institute of Criminology, sought to investigate why so many sexual assault complaints – about two-thirds of those made to police in Queensland – were withdrawn, not substantiated or considered unsolved.

Interviews with detectives and others paint a grim picture about the experience of making a sexual assault complaint. One told the researchers that police interviews with victim-survivors were often conducted in “the room where the admin ladies sit”.
“Previous to that we used the ladies’ change room,” the officer said.
Another said: “We have victims of rapes coming into this office with other officers here answering phones.”

Detectives told researchers they were struggling to cope with heavy workloads and faced pressure to respond to matters that were considered political priorities, including youth crime, property crime and domestic and family violence.
“The serious jobs like sexual assault, they’re life changing, life-ruining stuff,” one detective said.
“And they’re not getting any attention at all because some kid walked into a bottle shop and stole a bottle of vodka, and we end up dealing with that instead.”
Another said: “So you take a statement from them, and then something will pop up where someone’s running around with a gun, so now that’s your focus.
“A few jobs like this back up, and then all of a sudden … it’s been 12 months.”

Investigators told the researchers that cases, particularly relating to historical sexual offence allegations, had been “sitting there for yonks” and “get put on the backburner because there’s just too much other work”.
Officers spoke about being in a state of permanent “stress response” because of the intense workload.

“When we’re in a stress response, we don’t act with our compassion systems in place; neurobiologically, your empathy system is offline,” an officer said. “The police are under so much stress and then we’re asking them to perform in a trauma informed victim-centric way.”

The researchers found that officers who investigated sexual assault offences were often generalist detectives required to also handle property crime or complex fraud cases. Their data showed that when investigations were handled by officers who had specialist training in sexual offences, case attrition rates decreased.
Some sexual assault support service workers raised concerns about police responses in interviews with researchers.
One spoke about a victim-survivor who “presented very heightened to police [and] basically was told settle down or we’ll arrest you”.

Detectives described difficulties obtaining rape kit forensic tests at public hospitals, including cases where they had to drive victim-survivors up to seven hours for a test, or where qualified hospital staff were not available to conduct tests.

“We’ve got a hospital that is literally 250m from the police station,” one officer said. “If somebody turns up at 2am reporting a rape, you’re not getting them back here until at least 9am in the morning.”
Another said: “We’ve been told there is someone on call 24 hours every day of the year to do the kits locally. But they’re not picking up the phone.”
after newsletter promotion
In one case recounted by a detective, a victim-survivor waited 14 hours in an emergency ward and was then told to “do their own swabs”.
“This is a regular occurrence.”

Detectives working on sexual assault cases also expressed frustration about the decisions of prosecutors not to proceed with cases in court; they said the DPP did not have the same accountability measures as the police.
“The DPP get rid of cases by saying ‘I don’t believe what she said because they didn’t act how a rape victim should’,” one officer said.
Another said: “Victim trust is affected when they’re reassured by police that it’s a good case, and then the DPP decides no.”

The study looked at more than 19,000 sexual assault allegations made to police between 2018 and 2022. It found that only 36% were considered “solved”. Of the remainder, 31% were “withdrawn by the victim-survivor”, 11% were deemed by police to be not substantiated, and 22% considered “unsolved”.

The chief executive of the Queensland Sexual Assault Network (Qsan), Angela Lynch, said data showing nearly one-third of sexual violence cases were withdrawn was “very concerning” and pointed to “larger systemic issues and barriers for victims”.

“These issues unfortunately are consistent with frontline sexual violence worker and victim-survivor experience. Delays in the system are a huge impediment to victim-survivors being able to continue to engage and these, along with other issues, can leave [them] with an impression their case is not a priority.”
She said Qsan supported a specialist response to sexual violence, including by police.

The authors of the new report – titled Attrition of sexual offences in police investigations: Exploring police, case and system factors that lead to withdrawn and unfounded outcomes – made a number of recommendations, including that police should “invest in specialist domestic, family and sexual violence investigation units”.
The Queensland police service recently closed its specialist domestic and family violence and vulnerable persons command.

The report researchers also argued that general duties officers should receive “foundational” training about sexual offences. They said officers and prosecutors should be required to advise victim-survivors personally when a case is not proceeding to prosecution.
The Queensland police service was contacted and offered the opportunity to comment.

articles.title: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?
articles.summary: Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

image.caption: The Berlin Wall came down on November 9, 1989Image: Norbert Michalke/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the wall. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.
Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.
Winter shoes? Candy!
Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.
In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.
The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalls. "I think it was just too fast for people."

blocks.caption: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, author Lea Streisand was finally able to visit her great-grandmother in the western part of BerlinImage: Marlene Gawrisch

blocks.text: The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Vorpommern, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany’s most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.
"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in her: "I quickly realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalls. "That made me afraid."

blocks.caption: Photo artist Simon Menner is interested in how images are instrumentalized in advertising, propaganda and warfareImage: Simon Menner

blocks.text: Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As he put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.
In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."
The Stasi's photo treasure trove

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns him — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.
His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Sometimes eerie, sometimes curious, even absurd.

blocks.caption: Before searching an apartment, the Stasi would take Polaroid photographs so that they could subsequently restore the rooms to the state in which they had found themImage: Simon Menner/BStU 2013

blocks.text: Simon Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success."
In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany’s past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

According to Lea Streisand, literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she says. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Anke Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

blocks.caption: 'May Day' from the comic book 'Comrade Cuckoo' by Anke FeuchtenbergerImage: Anke Feuchtenberger

blocks.text: The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.
The artist says she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the Wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty. Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, says Feuchtenberger.
What does the future hold?

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than the West German man. "In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," says Simon Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he said, referring to the recent election successes of far-right party Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Anke Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explains. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world. Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border: "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want." That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," thinks Lea Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
articles.summary: The Greek coastguard says it has rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals.

blocks.text: At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.
The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.
Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.
One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".
The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.
The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.
More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.
The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.
Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.

Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is embroiled in a spying scandal. Could the AI chipmaker survive without him?

image.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, on Oct. 21. As the CEO is investigated to determine whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, analysts worry what the future would look like for Nvidia if Huang had to step down. (Markus Schre

blocks.text: Business·New

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has helmed the company since starting it in 1993, guiding it from a graphics card maker to the AI behemoth it is today. But with an investigation now underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and no clear successor in sight, analysts say a change at the top — if it were deemed necessary — would be massive.
Analysts say change at the top would be a big shakeup, but company would go on
Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.

But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.

The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.

items: Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims

blocks.text: In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.
"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.

Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.
"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."
'The king of tech'

Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.

An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon, Meta, Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.
Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.

items: Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair
Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky

blocks.text: From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.
"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.

Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang
Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.

Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.
The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.
Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.
No clear successor
With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.
"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.
If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.
But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.
The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That
"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.
While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.
O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.
Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang, O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.

Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.

"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: House pushes thousands more multi-purpose buildings. Are they really needed?
articles.summary: House appropriations panel senior vice chairperson Albert Garcia says multi-purpose buildings can be used for Zumba, basketball games, and even as evacuation centers

blocks.text: LOWER CHAMBER. The House of Representatives Session Hall.
House of Representatives' Facebook page
House appropriations panel senior vice chairperson Albert Garcia says multi-purpose buildings can be used for Zumba, basketball games, and even as evacuation centers

items: The House of Representatives has approved an additional P42.7 billion for multi-purpose buildings in the proposed 2027 national budget, raising the total allocation to P83.7 billion.
Lawmakers argue that the funding is necessary to meet the needs of the country's 42,000 barangays, with multi-purpose buildings serving various community functions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
How many multi-purpose buildings does the country need?
For members of the House of Representatives, apparently, thousands more.
In the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, lawmakers inserted an additional P42.7 billion for multi-purpose buildings.
That brings the allocation from the P41 billion proposed by the Marcos administration to P83.7 billion — more than double the proposal! The sum is enough to fund an estimated 5,765 buildings.
A lot, right?
For congressmen, not quite.

House appropriations committee senior vice chairperson Albert Garcia and other lawmakers defended the allocation, arguing that the country has tens of thousands of barangays that need such facilities.
“How many barangays do we have? 42,000 barangays. That’s a mere 10% (referring to the allocation for multi-purpose buildings) of the need of barangays across the nation,” Garcia said.
Lawmakers also claimed that requests from local government units for multi-purpose buildings continue to pour into their offices.
So, what exactly do barangays need all these buildings for?
Garcia said multi-purpose buildings can serve several purposes, from covered courts and daycare centers to classrooms and venues for community meetings.

“Alam ‘nyo po sa mga probinsiya at barangay na nasa labas ng Metro Manila, napakaimportante po nitong multi-purpose building,” Garcia said. (In provinces and barangays outside Metro Manila, multi-purpose buildings are very important.)
An analysis by People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, however, showed that most of the allocation in the previous years for multi-purpose buildings were in Metro Manila.
He cited covered courts as an example, saying these can host Zumba sessions, barangay consultations, and basketball games for young people.

“Halimbawa, covered court. Diyan po nag-Zu-Zumba ’yung ating mga kababayan sa barangay na ’yun for healthy lifestyle. Diyan po nagme-meeting si kapitan para konsultahin ang kanyang mga ka-barangay. Diyan po nagba-basketball tuwing hapon ’yung ating mga kabataan para umiwas sa droga, para maging mas malusog kaysa puro gadgets na lang ginagawa ng ating mga kabataan,” he said.

(For example, a covered court. That’s where our constituents in the barangay hold Zumba sessions to promote a healthy lifestyle. It’s where the barangay captain holds meetings to consult with residents. It’s also where young people play basketball every afternoon to keep them away from drugs and encourage them to stay healthy, rather than spend all their time on gadgets.)

blocks.caption: House pushes thousands more multi-purpose buildings. Are they really needed?

blocks.text: But not everyone is convinced that the billions in additional funding are adequately justified.
PBC and BetterGovPH flagged the multi-purpose building insertions, saying publicly available supporting documents were lacking to establish the need for these projects.
Fuentebella, however, defended the insertions, insisting they went through the proper process.

“Lahat po nito nanggaling sa request nila. Hindi lang po sa kagustuhan ng mga kongresista. So it’s a bottom-up budgeting ang ginagawa natin,” Fuentebella said. (All of these came from requests made by the communities themselves, not simply from the congressmen’s own preferences. So what we are practicing is bottom-up budgeting.)
He said that there are documents to support these projects, but these have yet to be seen by the public.
This isn’t the first time Congress has substantially increased funding for these projects.
In 2026, lawmakers more than doubled the P29.7 billion allocation proposed in the National Expenditure Program, raising it to P79.9 billion.
Budget analysis of PBC and BetterGovPH also showed that the government has allocated P739.6 billion for 79,970 multi-purpose building projects from 2015 to 2026.
Perhaps, they want more multi-purpose buildings to put their names or initials? – Rappler.com

items: Ateneo head coach Louie Alas has been suspended for two games due to unsportsmanlike conduct and two infractions during a recent game against UP.
The suspension will affect upcoming games against Adamson and UST, crucial for Ateneo's chances of making the UAAP Final Four.
Alas has a history of infractions, including a previous automatic suspension last month, and Ateneo has the option to appeal the current suspension.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo’s woes continue amid a crucial stretch in the Blue Eagles’ UAAP men’s basketball Final Four chase.
The UAAP suspended Ateneo head coach Louie Alas for two games “following the accumulation of two infractions” and his “unsportsmanlike conduct,” the league said in a statement on Monday, November 9.
Alas will serve his suspension on Wednesday, November 11, when the Blue Eagles battle the Adamson Falcons, and on Sunday, November 15, when they take on the UST Growling Tigers.
The penalty stemmed from two incidents involving Alas during a tense matchup last Saturday, November 7, where the Maroons outlasted the Blue Eagles, 82-74.
Right at the buzzer, Alas confronted the UP side before cooler heads stepped in to prevent the situation from escalating.

“With less than a second remaining, Alas entered the court, pointed at UP’s Jacob Bayla, and cursed at him following the latter’s dunk,” the league said in a statement. “He again pointed at and cursed at the UP player during the post-game handshake.”
The league said the Ateneo mentor also “engaged in an exchange with UP assistant coach Christian Luanzon despite attempts by UP coaches to pacify him.”
“The Commissioner’s Office determined that his actions escalated tensions between the two teams and risked a potential altercation.”
Prior to the end-game commotion, Alas entered the court at the 3:55 mark of the first quarter, complaining about a non-call.
Alas “remained on the playing court despite being warned by the nearest referee to return to the sideline,” the league said.
He was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike behavior during the game.
The UAAP cited another Alas infraction during Ateneo’s loss to UST, 80-68, on October 17.

“At the 5:15 mark of the third quarter, he attempted to distract UST’s Amiel Acido as the latter attempted a corner three-pointer. After Acido converted the shot, Alas touched the back of the UST player,” the statement said.

“Although the incident was missed by the game officials, the Commissioner’s Office reviewed the play and imposed the appropriate disciplinary sanction under the UAAP House Rules and applicable FIBA regulations.”
Alas’ suspension comes at a crucial time as the Blue Eagles, running fifth with a 5-6 record, try to chase a Final Four spot with just three games left in the second round.
Ateneo can appeal the suspension.
Last October, Alas also served an automatic one-game suspension after accumulating three infractions. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte: Gov't officials should not pick fights with other countries
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte cautioned the Philippine government against picking fights with other countries, including China.

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte cautioned the Philippine government against picking fights with other countries, including China.

Speaking at a gathering with Overseas Filipino Workers in Hong Kong on Sunday, the Vice President suggested that resolving issues, such as the maritime dispute between China and the Philippines, is better handled through diplomatic talks rather than heated exchanges online.

“Alam ninyo dapat kasi hindi nakikipag-away ang gobyerno o ang opsiyal ng gobyerno sa kahit na anong bansa dahil napaka-complicated ng relasyon ng dalawang bansa. Hindi lang siya isang bagay lang, maraming aspeto ang relasyon ng Pilipinas sa bawat bansa,” Duterte said in a 24 Oras report of Marisol Abdurahman on Monday.

(The government or a government official should not pick a fight with any country because bilateral relations are very complicated. It is not just a single matter; there are many aspects to the Philippines' relationship with every nation.)
“Bumuo ng isang team ng mga diplomats at yon ang ipadala mo kung saan man nila gusto makipag-usap, sila dapat yung nag-uusap,” she added.
(Form a team of diplomats and send them wherever they need to negotiate; they should be the ones talking.)
Duterte said that in relations with other countries, national interest must always be the priority.
She also pointed out that failing to maintain good relations with China could adversely affect the livelihoods of many Filipinos.

“Dapat iniisip ng pamahalaan ‘Gaano ba kalaki ang baril ko? Gaano ba kalaki ang baril ng kalaban?’ Ulo pa lang, pinukpok na yung maliit mo na baril. Dapat balanse, hindi siya basta na lang tira nang tira lalo na ‘pag malaki ang baril ng kalaban mo,” the Vice President added.

(The government should consider, ‘How big is my gun? How big is the adversary's gun?’ Before you can even react, your small gun has already been crushed. There must be balance; you can’t just keep taking shots indiscriminately, especially when your opponent has a bigger gun.)
'Philippines isn't the aggressor'
In response to Duterte, Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, the Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, clarified that no one is suggesting the Philippines go to war with China.

Tarriela said the country's strongest defense in its territorial claims is not armed force, but the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the 2016 Arbitral Award it won, which recognized Philippine sovereignty in the West Philippine Sea.

“Walang nagsasabing makikipag-giyera tayo. Hindi laki ng braso ang laban natin kung ang UNCLOS, ang 2016 Arbitral Award na tayo ang nanalo… Kapag laki ng kamao ang nagde-define kung ano ang tama, tama nga si [Chinese Ambassador] Jing Quan, at wala nang silbi ang international law,” Tarriela wrote in a post.

(No one is saying we should go to war. Our fight is not determined by muscle power, but by UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award that we won... If brute force defined what is right, then Jing Quan would be correct, and international law would be useless.)

He also emphasized that the Philippines is not the aggressor taking indiscriminate shots, pointing to China's use of water cannons and dangerous maneuvers against Philippine authorities and Filipino fishers at sea.
He added that sending diplomats has long been the practice, but it is the other side that fails to comply with agreements.
“China po ang gumagamit ng water cannon at dangerous maneuvers. Ang PCG at BFAR ay pinoprotektahan lamang ang ating mga mangingisda sa sarili natin [Exclusive Economic Zone],” Tarriela said.
(It is China that uses water cannons and performs dangerous maneuvers. The PCG and BFAR are merely protecting our fishermen within our own Exclusive Economic Zone.)
In an interview, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) stated that all government officials—whether civilian or uniformed—are expected to adhere to the directives of the President.

While naming no specific individuals, the DFA noted that recent public statements by certain officials inappropriately combined distinct aspects of foreign policy, emphasizing that official diplomatic actions require a clear boundary.

“It is therefore regrettable that recent public commentary made by certain government officials have incorrectly merged three distinct elements: documentary evidence, public rhetoric and official diplomatic messaging. Government statecraft requires clear distinctions among these instruments,” the DFA said. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Prosecution flags defense witness's 25-day trip to China
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Monday flagged a 25-day trip to China taken by Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin in January this year.

blocks.text: VP SARA IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published November 9, 2026 9:10pm

The House prosecution panel on Monday flagged a 25-day trip to China taken by defense witness and Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin last January, saying such a lengthy stay is not normal for a "simple tourist."

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas raised the alarm after Adalin repeatedly dodged questions both from the prosecution and the Senator-judges about his frequent chips to China, including a supposedly all-expenses-paid trip last November.
Luistro said that Adalin was part of a delegation who went to China and stayed there from January 5 to 30 this year.
Luistro said the delegation entered via Beijing and left for Manila from Shanghai.
“Bakit kayo nandoon? Sinong nagbayad niyan? Why this long?” Luistro asked at a post-trial press conference.
(Why were they there? Who paid for that?)

“That’s not normal for a simple tourist na bibisita sa ibang bansa [visiting another country]. Twenty-five days? Hotel accommodations alone in a two-star or three-star hotel could have cost more than P100,000,” Luistro added.
Adalin initially said he could not recall a trip or whether the Chinese government had paid for it.
But amid repeated questioning, Adalin later told the Senate impeachment court that he indeed went to China and paid his own expenses.
“Actually, pina-confirm ko po sa opisina. Indeed, nag-travel po kami sa China,” Adalin said during the questioning of Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo.
(I confirmed it with my office. Indeed, we traveled to China.)
Tulfo also cited that based on Immigration records, Adalin also traveled to Hong Kong, Thailand and Australia.
Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros later asked Adalin if the went to Beijing, Shanghai or Fujian which three major cities in China, but Adalin replied that he does not enjoy traveling that much.
“Actually, I’m not keen on traveling, Your Honor. Kaya hindi ko na mine-memorize ‘yung pinupuntahan,” Adalin said.
(Which is why I didn't memorize the places we have been.)
Hontiveros then shot back “You're not keen on traveling pero nag-travel po kayo?.”
(You are not keen on traveling but you traveled anyway?)
Adalin replied, "yes, you’re correct.” — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Nine foreigners caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
articles.summary: Police declined to disclose their nationalities but said none of them lived in South Africa.

blocks.text: Nine foreigners have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
The group is accused of contravening South Africa's laws, which outlaw mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said the group were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.

The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
Authorities declined to disclose the group's nationalities but confirmed that none of them resided in South Africa.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In February, Ghana said that 55 of its citizens had been killed in the conflict, with 272 believed to have been lured to fight since the war started in 2022.
The same month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
The nine arrested are expected to appear in court either later on Monday or Tuesday.

articles.title: Prosecution: Defense's first witness a 'weakness' amid discrepancies in testimony
articles.summary: The defense's first witness turned out to be "a weakness" for them due to a testimony peppered with inconsistencies, the House prosecution team said Monday.

blocks.text: The first witness presented by the defense team in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial turned out to be "a weakness" for them due to a testimony peppered with inconsistencies, the House prosecution team said Monday.

The prosecution team made the observation after Davao City assessor and engineer Jaime Adalin testified that the residential lot with an acquisition cost of 10 million under Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) 146-2024-010775 is the same property declared by the Duterte in her 2024 and 2025 SALN even if the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR) for the said property showed an acquisition cost of P6 million in 2024, not P10 million.
House prosecutor Joel Chua said that the discrepancy is just one of the many red flags.

“In the eCAR, the acquisition cost is P6 million, but under the SALN, the acquisition cost is P10 million. Secondly, eCAR states that the property is a lot with improvement, but for the SALN, it just states lot. Thirdly, SALN declaration states residential lot, but when the prosecution showed the current photo of property with a commercial building, nung tinatanong siya, biglang hindi niya na masagot kung ito ay commercial,” Chua said in a press conference.
(When shown a photo, suddenly, he could not say whether it was a commercial establishment.)

An eCAR is issued by the Bureau of Internal Revenue once the property has been transferred and corresponding dues were paid by the new owner, in this case, as a result of a property sale to the Vice President’s husband, Manases Carpio.
The SALN of the Vice President, on the other hand, is a joint filing with Carpio.
“Lumalabas po yung pinresenta po kanina ng depensa na witness ay lumalabas na isang weakness,” Chua added.
(What emerged here is that the defense witness turned out to be a weakness.)

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas, for her part, said that Adalin was wrong to use the property’s title in concluding that it was the same property declared by the Vice President as an asset in her 2024 and 2025 SALN because the land title and SALN requires different information.

“Our [prosecution] reference, of course, is the SALN. And the description in the SALN only states the barangay, assessed value, the fair market value, and even the acquisition cost. There is no way [for the witness] to verify because the [land] title provides for different references. The [land] title makes use of the technical description which was never contained in the SALN,” Luistro pointed out.

“How do you compare the description in the SALN with a different mode of description in other documents? What is clear is that the description of the property in the title is entirely different from the description of the property in the SALN,” she added.
Private prosecutor Benjamin Tolosa, Jr., who conducted the cross-examination on Adalin, stressed that the discrepancies in the amounts is a clear stain on his testimony.

“How can you say that they're the same considering these discrepancies? And with respect on the similarity of fair market value and assessed value, it's possible that other properties in the same area may have the same fair market value and assessed value, as noted by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian,” he said.

Tolosa was referring to Gatchalian questioning Adalin’s conclusion that the P6 million property acquired by the Vice President’s husband in 2024 is the same P10 million declared asset of the Vice President in 2024 and 2025 even if the SALN entries on the said property does not state a title number.
"Wala naman pong nakasulat na title number. Wala rin pong nakasulat na tax declaration number," Gatchalian pointed out.
(There is no title number and tax declaration in the SALN.)

Gatchalian then asked Adalin if it is possible that other properties near the subject property have the same assessed value and fair market value, considering that nearby parcels appeared to have similar shapes based on the maps presented by the defense and the prosecution.
Adalin replied, "Yes, most probably, Your Honor." — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Lights go out at Russia’s Novaya Gazeta, after years of defiant reporting
articles.summary: 'We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has effectively ceased to function,' says Novaya Gazeta co-founder Dmitry…

blocks.text: PRESS FREEDOM. Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta, holds a poster in support of jailed reporters outside the outlet's office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a relentless campaign by the authorities, in Moscow, Russia, on November 9, 2026.
Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters

'We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has effectively ceased to function,' says Novaya Gazeta co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a co-winner of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize

items: Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta ceased operations on November 9 due to state pressure, marking the end of a significant independent news outlet.
Co-founder Dmitry Muratov emphasized the importance of free speech and human rights, criticizing the Kremlin for suppressing dissent and blaming it for the ongoing war in Ukraine.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MOSCOW, Russia – Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta wound up its operations on Monday, November 9, and quit its central Moscow office, bowing to what it said was a campaign of state pressure that had made it impossible to carry on reporting.
Its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, addressing journalists who gathered to witness the newspaper’s closure, issued an impassioned plea for free speech and human rights in wartime Russia.
“Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today,” he said.
“We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has effectively ceased to function.”
The closure marks the end of one of Russia’s most influential independent news outlets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was part of a “rotational process” in a fiercely competitive media environment.

The newspaper, renowned for fearless reporting that led to six of its journalists being murdered over the years, was founded by Muratov and the last Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, using money from Gorbachev’s 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.

Inspired by Gorbachev’s vision of “glasnost,” or openness, it became one of Russia’s most influential newspapers and defenders of democracy, with investigations into corruption and critical coverage of politics.

After President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale war with Ukraine in 2022 and Russia imposed tight censorship laws, the paper halted its print edition but continued to publish online, becoming a refuge for independent journalists who chose to remain in the country.

But it announced late last month that it would have to close after it was designated a “foreign agent” and ordered to vacate its offices, and banks stopped processing reader donations on which it relied for financial survival.
Muratov, a co-winner of the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, said people needed to understand that it was the Kremlin that was to blame for waging the war and suppressing free speech.

“We cannot blame the citizens themselves for this — especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation. I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people,” he said.
He called for a broader ceasefire in Ukraine following a six-day truce in one area brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in late October.
Muratov also urged the release of what he said were around 4,000 political prisoners in Russia.

The Kremlin defends the need for censorship laws, denies there are any political prisoners and says that Russia is taking necessary action at a time of war to prosecute people engaged in subversive activity.

It was unclear whether the newspaper would attempt to regroup and publish in another form. In a long article on its website, describing its final weeks, journalist Irina Vorobyova was quoted as saying its spirit would survive like a “good virus.”
“Not even a nuclear explosion could destroy it. It will continue in everyone who was part of it,” she said. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala continues to wade through uncharted waters in her blossoming tennis career as she notched yet another career-high world rank of No. 15 in the latest WTA rankings released on Monday, November 9.

With this newest rise on the women’s tennis leaderboards, the 21-year-old Eala has now traded places with Japanese star Naomi Osaka, who took Eala’s old No. 17 spot, while Romania’s Sorana Cirstea sits between them at No. 16.

Like her rise to No. 15, Eala’s switch with Osaka is a historic career feat in itself, as the Filipina sensation is now the second-highest-ranked Asian in the world, trailing only world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan.

Both Osaka and Eala have since ended their respective 2026 seasons, with the Japanese standout bowing out of the Toray Pan Pacific Open Round of 16 last November 1, and the Filipina falling to American Claire Liu in a one-sided Hong Kong Open final last November 8.

“This season, it hass changed my life. It has changed my life for the better,” Eala said at the Hong Kong Open awarding ceremony alongside Liu, who rose 33 spots from world No. 102 to 69 with her title win.

“I’m incredibly proud of the work we’ve put in this year, and we’re the only ones who truly know what it took to arrive to this point in our journey,” added Eala, whose ranking surged this year after a historic title run at the Washington Open, a WTA 500 event.
“Thank you so, so much. This is only the beginning. And this one, like all of them, is ours. Thank you, everyone.”
Joining Rybakina, Eala, and Osaka as Asia’s top five are top Chinese stars Qinwen Zheng at world No. 22 and Xinyu Wang at No. 38.

Completing the world’s top 5, meanwhile, are Rybakina, Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus, Mirra Andreeva of Russia, and familiar Eala rivals Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula of the United States at No. 4 and 5, respectively.

Eala soon heads back to the Philippines to further celebrate her career highs and 2026 season overall with a big homecoming event, “Alex Eala Live: Game. Set. Celebrate,” at the 55,000-seater Philippine Arena on December 8.
There, Eala will play Southeast Asia’s second-best tennis star, world No. 60 Janice Tjen of Indonesia, in a marquee exhibition. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Germany: CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president
articles.summary: The steering committtee of the CDU have announced Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner as presidential candidate. This gives her a good chance of becoming the first woman to occupy the role.

image.caption: Aigner is currently the speaker of Bavaria's state parliamentImage: Alexandra Beier/AFP

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday confirmed that they would be putting forward Ilse Aigner as a candidate to be Germany's next head of state.

Aigner's own CSU, the CDU's Bavarian sister party, already supports her candidacy — and the federal coalition partners the Social Democrats have also made clear they would endorse her nomination if the conservatives agree on it.
This means the 61-year-old has a good chance of taking up the largely ceremonial role when the special committee that elects a German president convenes in late January.
While Angela Merkel famously served as the country's most powerful politician for more than a decade, Germany has never had a female head of state.
Could Ilse Aigner become Germany's first female head of state?
How did Aigner come to be nominated?
Aigner's chances at the nomination had been gathering momentum for some time now, with various government politicians including Chancellor Merz saying they'd favor a female candidate.
The CSU had in particular lobbied for the 13th post-war German president to be the first one from the Bavarian party and the first woman.

Reports that Merz would suggest Aigner as a candidate to the steering committee first emerged on Friday, and were then confirmed by participants when the party leadership convened for two days of talks on Sunday.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second five-year term comes to an end next March. The special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects a German president therefore convenes in late January to choose his successor.
The committee — comprising 1,260 people in all — is made up of federal and state lawmakers, and sometimes municipal officials and others from public life.
SPD leader and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has voiced support for her nomination.

The CDU/CSU and SPD command a majority in the committee, and it's also possible that Green party politicians might support Aigner. This means her chances of selection seem strong, at least barring unexpected developments.

blocks.caption: Frank-Walter Steinmeier's decade as president comes to an end early next year, meaning political parties are seeking a succeessorImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who is Ilse Aigner?
Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.
Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.
She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.
She's currently the speaker or president of the state legislature in Bavaria, a role she has held since 2018.

articles.title: EU aims to pick new ECB chief by year-end
articles.summary: Christine Lagarde's early decision to step down as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of…

image.caption: The successors for the ECB's top jobs would likely be negotiated among the main eurozone countriesImage: KIRILL KUDRYAVTSEV/AFP

blocks.text: The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.
Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, has announced on October 29 that she is stepping down prematurely from the position, nine months ⁠before ⁠the end of her term.
Lagarde's early decision to step down makes the schedule tight because leaders must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board ​within months.
"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
Who pays for Europe’s economic independence?

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in ​the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.
Who are the candidates?
The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International ​Settlements, Pablo ‌Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.
The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.
Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'
Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position", referring to his long-standing experience.
"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.
EU wants to attract European savers to boost bloc's economy

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfil this position."

Heinen also ​said countries should ‌not see the ECB leadership contest as ​one between northern ⁠and southern European countries, or as ⁠an "​opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.
A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel ‌Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, ​whose term ends ⁠in May 2027.
The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the ⁠main eurozone countries — ​France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.
The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.
Can Europe's economy survive in a new world order?
"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.
Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.
"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

articles.title: Senators urge Marcos to declare state of calamity in Super El Niño-hit areas
articles.summary: The Senate resolution notes that despite over 100 cities and towns declaring a state of calamity as of October 2026, only one in five farmers has received aid

blocks.text: EL NINO. A store attendant at Trabajo Market in Manila assists a customer purchasing a water container on October 6, 2026. According to the vendor, there has been a slight increase in customers buying buckets, water containers, and other vessels for water storage following reports on the effects of El Niño.
Rappler
The Senate resolution notes that despite over 100 cities and towns declaring a state of calamity as of October 2026, only one in five farmers has received aid

items: Twenty senators have urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity due to the impacts of Super El Niño, which would allow access to necessary funds.

The declaration would enable measures such as price ceilings on basic goods, monitoring against hoarding, and funding for infrastructure repairs, particularly to support the agricultural sector facing significant losses.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines – Twenty senators on Monday, November 9, have called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected or threatened by the Super El Niño, allowing access to funds to combat the weather phenomenon’s impact on the country.

Under Republic Act No. 10121, the declaration of a state of calamity mandates remedial measures such as the imposition of a price ceiling on basic necessities and commodities, monitoring and prevention of hoarding and profiteering activities, programming of funds for the repair and upgrading of public infrastructure, and the granting of no-interest loans to affected communities.

Upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), the senators, through Proposed Senate Resolution No. 765, urged the President to declare a state of calamity to address challenges being faced primarily by the agricultural sector.

Among those who signed the resolution were Senate President Win Gatchalian, Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto, and senators Kiko Pangilinan, Migz Zubiri, Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros, JV Ejercito, Lito Lapid, Joel Villanueva, Erwin Tulfo, Raffy Tulfo, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Alan Peter Cayetano, Pia Cayetano, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, Bong Go, Camille Villar, and Mark Villar.

According to the Department of Agriculture, the country has reported P6.87 billion in agricultural losses across 249,028 hectares as of September 26 — nearly half of the recorded losses during the 2023-2024 El Niño.

“Planting season ngayon sa ating mga palayan at kailangan ng tubig. Kailangan mag-plant din tayo ng mga remedial measure tulad ng pag-impose ng price ceilings at laban sa overpricing, profiteering, at hoarding,” Pangilinan said.
(It’s planting season in our rice fields, and we need water. We also need to plant remedial measures, such as imposing price ceilings and policies against overpricing, profiteering, and hoarding)

On November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean and is expected to persist until the first half of 2027.

According to PAGASA, the weather phenomenon will potentially reach its peak by the end of 2026, increasing the likelihood of rainfall deficits and, consequently, raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.

“Based on the latest drought assessment, five provinces experienced meteorological drought, 11 provinces were under dry spell, and 10 provinces experienced dry conditions in October 2026,” PAGASA Administrator Nathaniel Servando said in a statement.

The Senate resolution stated that while more than a hundred cities and municipalities have declared a state of calamity, the Department of Agriculture has managed to provide aid to only 2.53 million out of 11.12 million target beneficiaries. This means only one in five farmers are getting the help they need amid drought and dry conditions.
According to the senators, around P39 billion is available under the country’s disaster response fund. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global…

image.caption: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993Image: Joyce N. Boghosian/White House/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.
The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believes she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.
What has Nvidia and the US government said?

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.
Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

blocks.caption: Nvidia chips are used to build and run AI applications Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."
The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.
While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.
"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."
Why it matters for Nvidia

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.
"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

blocks.caption: The sale of Nvidia chips to China is a major political sorepointImage: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, says the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Jensen Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.
"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."
The tangled China-Nvidia web
Nvidia and Huang's attitude towards China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed their sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-licence review. Beijing has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.
Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

blocks.caption: Nvidia is at the center of the US-China rivalry in AI Image: Huang Jingwen/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials, who fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost their domestic AI sector, lead to their AI models catching up with the leading US models and could be used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.
What China hopes to gain
Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Richard Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also casts doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.
"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

blocks.caption: While China has made advances it AI, it lacks advanced chips Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

blocks.text: The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom, thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.
Its valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.
Edited by Nik Martin
